summary.text: The gamma quotient is rewritten using factorials and double factorials, split by the parity of the index, and stripped of all factors divisible by \(p\), leaving products arranged in residue blocks modulo \(q=p^r\). Expanding shifted blocks through degree two modulo \(q^3\), the requisite sums of inverse units and inverse squares vanish; for odd half-blocks a doubling symmetry supplies the compensating powers of \(2\), after which the block powers cancel and the unit denominator can be cancelled.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(N)=\frac{\Gamma(9N+1)\Gamma(2N+1)\Gamma(3N/2+1)}
 {\Gamma(9N/2+1)\Gamma(4N+1)\Gamma(3N+1)\Gamma(N+1)}.
\]
We assume, as in the statement being proved, that every \(a(N)\) is an integer. We prove that if \(p\geq 5\) is prime and \(n,r\geq1\), then
\[
 a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]

Throughout, \(m!!\) denotes the double factorial. Congruences involving products of residue classes will generally be carried out in \(\mathbb Z/q^3\mathbb Z\), where eventually \(q\) is a positive power of \(p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Unit sums and truncated products

We first establish the modular product facts used in both parity cases.

Let \(q>1\) be coprime to \(6\), and let \(G=(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times\). For \(u\in G\), write \(\bar u\in\{1,\ldots,q-1\}\) for its standard representative. Multiplication by any fixed element of \(G\) permutes \(G\). Consequently,
\[
 \sum_{u\in G}u=\sum_{u\in G}2u=2\sum_{u\in G}u
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z.
\]
Thus \(\sum u=0\). Similarly,
\[
 \sum_{u\in G}u^2=\sum_{u\in G}(2u)^2=4\sum_{u\in G}u^2.
\]
Since \(3\) is invertible modulo \(q\), this gives
\[
 \sum_{u\in G}u^2=0.                                      \tag{1}
\]
Inversion also permutes \(G\), so the same identities hold with \(u^{-1}\) in place of \(u\).

We shall repeatedly use the following elementary truncated-product identity. For a finite set \(I\), elements \(f_i\) of a commutative ring, and an element \(x\) satisfying \(x^3=0\),
\[
 \prod_{i\in I}(1+xf_i)
 =1+x\sum_i f_i+x^2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subset I,\ i\ne j}f_if_j. \tag{2}
\]
Here the final sum is over unordered two-element subsets. This follows simply by expanding the product: terms involving three or more selected factors contain \(x^3\). If
\[
 P(f)=\sum_{i<j}f_if_j,
\]
then
\[
 2P(f)=\left(\sum_i f_i\right)^2-\sum_i f_i^2.             \tag{3}
\]

We need one slightly stronger inverse-sum fact. Lift each \(u\in G\) to the unit \(\bar u\) modulo \(q^2\). Then
\[
 \sum_{u\in G}\bar u^{-1}=0\pmod {q^2}.                   \tag{4}
\]
To prove this, pair the terms indexed by \(u\) and \(-u\). Their standard representatives satisfy
\[
 \bar u+\overline{-u}=q.
\]
Therefore, in \(\mathbb Z/q^2\mathbb Z\),
\[
 \bar u^{-1}+\overline{-u}^{-1}
 =q(\bar u\,\overline{-u})^{-1}.
\]
If \(S=\sum \bar u^{-1}\) and
\(T=\sum(\bar u\,\overline{-u})^{-1}\), summing this identity and using that negation permutes \(G\) gives
\[
 2S=qT.                                                     \tag{5}
\]
Modulo \(q\),
\[
 T\equiv\sum_{u\in G}(u(-u))^{-1}
       =-\sum_{u\in G}u^{-2}=0
\]
by (1). Hence \(qT=0\pmod {q^2}\). Since \(2\) is invertible modulo \(q^2\), (5) proves (4).

Now lift \(u\) by the same standard representative to a unit modulo \(q^3\). Formula (4) says
\[
 q\sum_{u\in G}\bar u^{-1}=0\pmod {q^3}.                  \tag{6}
\]
Also (1), together with (3), gives
\[
 q^2P(\bar u^{-1}:u\in G)=0\pmod {q^3}.                   \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, modulo \(q\), both \(\sum u^{-1}\) and \(\sum u^{-2}\) vanish, so (3) shows that the pair sum vanishes modulo \(q\); multiplication by \(q^2\) then kills it modulo \(q^3\).

Define the complete unit block
\[
 U_q(j)=\prod_{u\in G}(\bar u+qj)\pmod {q^3}.
\]
Factoring out the units \(\bar u\) gives
\[
 U_q(j)=U_q(0)\prod_{u\in G}(1+qj\bar u^{-1}).
\]
Apply (2), noting that \((qj)^3=0\pmod {q^3}\). The linear term vanishes by (6), and the quadratic term by (7). Therefore
\[
 U_q(j)=U_q(0)\pmod {q^3}                                  \tag{8}
\]
for every \(j\geq0\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Ordinary factorials with their \(p\)-factors removed

For a prime \(p\), define
\[
 F_p(M)=\prod_{\substack{1\le i\le M\\p\nmid i}}i.
\]
The multiples of \(p\) among \(1,\ldots,pm\) are \(p,2p,\ldots,mp\), so
\[
 (pm)!=p^m m!F_p(pm).                                      \tag{9}
\]
Every \(F_p(M)\) is coprime to \(p\).

Let \(q=p^t\), where \(t\geq1\). Partition \(1,\ldots,qk\) into the intervals
\((qj,q(j+1)]\), \(0\leq j<k\). The factors in such an interval not divisible by \(p\) are exactly
\[
 qj+\bar u\qquad (u\in (\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times).
\]
Thus, by (8),
\[
 F_p(qk)\equiv U_q(0)^k\pmod {q^3}.                        \tag{10}
\]
The hypothesis \(p\geq5\) ensures that every power \(q\) of \(p\) is coprime to \(6\), as required above.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. The even-index factorial ratio

Define
\[
 E_N(k)=(18k)!(4k)!(3k)!,\qquad
 E_D(k)=(9k)!(8k)!(6k)!(2k)!.
\]
For later use also set
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 E_{U,N}(p,k)&=F_p(18pk)F_p(4pk)F_p(3pk),\\
 E_{U,D}(p,k)&=F_p(9pk)F_p(8pk)F_p(6pk)F_p(2pk).
 \end{aligned}

defining these products with the same arguments as in (9), equivalently
\(F_p(p(18k))\), and so forth.

Applying (9) to every factorial gives
\[
 E_N(pk)=P(p,k)E_N(k)E_{U,N}(p,k),
\]
\[
 E_D(pk)=P(p,k)E_D(k)E_{U,D}(p,k),                         \tag{11}
\]
with the same pure \(p\)-power on both sides, because
\[
18+4+3=9+8+6+2=25.
\]

Fix \(s\geq0\), put \(K=kp^s\), and put \(q=p^{s+1}\). Each argument appearing in \(E_{U,N}(p,K)\) or \(E_{U,D}(p,K)\) is of the form
\[
 p(cK)=q(ck).
\]
By (10), its residue modulo \(q^3\) is \(U_q(0)^{ck}\). Hence
\[
 E_{U,N}(p,K)\equiv U_q(0)^{(18+4+3)k}
 =U_q(0)^{25k},
\]
and
\[
 E_{U,D}(p,K)\equiv U_q(0)^{(9+8+6+2)k}
 =U_q(0)^{25k}\pmod {q^3}.                                \tag{12}
\]

Suppose integers \(z_0,z_1\) satisfy
\[
 z_0E_D(K)=E_N(K),\qquad z_1E_D(pK)=E_N(pK).               \tag{13}
\]
Use (11) in the second equality and cancel the common nonzero pure \(p\)-power. Then use the first equality and cancel the positive integer \(E_D(K)\). We get the exact equality
\[
 z_1E_{U,D}(p,K)=z_0E_{U,N}(p,K).                          \tag{14}
\]
The factor \(E_{U,D}(p,K)\) is coprime to \(p\), hence invertible modulo \(q^3\). By (12), (14) therefore yields
\[
 z_1\equiv z_0\pmod {q^3}.                               \tag{15}
\]
This proves the required quotient congruence for the even-index factorial ratio.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Odd residue blocks

The half-integer gamma factors require double factorials, so we now develop the corresponding odd-product version of (10).

Assume again that \(q>2\) and \((q,6)=1\), and let
\[
 H=\{u\in G:\bar u\text{ is odd}\}.
\]
Since \(q\) is odd, the standard representative of \(-u\) is \(q-\bar u\), whose parity is opposite to that of \(\bar u\). Thus negation bijects \(H\) with its complement. Since \((-u)^{-2}=u^{-2}\), equation (1) and invertibility of \(2\) imply
\[
 \sum_{u\in H}u^{-2}=0\pmod q.                            \tag{16}
\]
The same is true for the complementary half.

For \(j\geq0\), define in \(\mathbb Z/q^3\mathbb Z\)
\[
 A(j)=\prod_{u\in H}(1+qj\bar u^{-1}).
\]
Write
\[
 S=\sum_{u\in H}\bar u^{-1},\qquad
 P=\sum_{\{u,v\}\subset H}\bar u^{-1}\bar v^{-1}.
\]
By (2),
\[
 A(j)=1+qjS+q^2j^2P.                                      \tag{17}
\]
Equation (3) and (16) imply
\[
 q^2(S^2-2P)=0\pmod {q^3}.                                \tag{18}
\]
Substituting (17) and using \(q^3=0\) shows
\[
 A(j+k)=A(j)A(k),\qquad A(jk)=A(j)^k.                      \tag{19}
\]

We next evaluate \(A(1)\). Multiplication by \(2\) permutes \(G\). For every unit \(u\), reduction of \(2\bar u\) to its standard representative has the form
\[
 2\bar u=\overline{2u}+\begin{cases}q,&\overline{2u}\text{ odd},\\0,&\overline{2u}\text{ even}.
 \end{cases}                                               \tag{20}
\]
This is immediate by separating the cases \(2\bar u<q\) and \(2\bar u\geq q\). Multiply (20), in \(\mathbb Z/q^3\mathbb Z\), over all \(u\in G\). On the left one obtains
\(2^{|G|}\prod_u\bar u\). On the right, multiplication by \(2\) merely permutes the unit classes, and factoring each representative gives
\[
 \left(\prod_u\bar u\right)
 \prod_{u\in H}(1+q\bar u^{-1}).
\]
The common product of units can be cancelled. Hence
\[
 A(1)=2^{|G|},
\qquad A(2)=A(1)^2=2^{2|G|}.                              \tag{21}
\]

Define the odd half-block
\[
 D(j)=\prod_{u\in H}(\bar u+2qj).
\]
Factoring out \(D(0)\), then applying (19) and (21), gives
\[
 D(j)=D(0)A(2j)=D(0)\bigl(2^{2|G|}\bigr)^j.               \tag{22}
\]

For a full interval of length \(2q\), the odd representatives prime to \(p\) are naturally indexed by all \(u\in G\): use
\[
 r_u=\bar u+\begin{cases}0,&\bar u\text{ odd},\\q,&\bar u\text{ even}.
\end{cases}

define
\[
 C=\prod_{u\in G}r_u,
\qquad B=\prod_{u\in G}\bar u,
\qquad e=2^{|G|}
\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/q^3\mathbb Z.
\]
We claim
\[
 Ce=B.                                                      \tag{23}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 C=B\prod_{\bar u\text{ even}}(1+q\bar u^{-1}).
\]
The product over the odd representatives is \(A(1)=e\). The product over all representatives is \(1\), by the complete-block calculation (8) with \(j=1\). Thus the products over the odd and even halves multiply to \(1\), and (23) follows.

We also need invariance under shifts by \(2q\). The inverse of \(r_u\) modulo \(q^3\) can be written explicitly. If \(z=\bar u^{-1}\), then
\[
 r_u^{-1}=\begin{cases}
z,&\bar u\text{ odd},\\
z-qz^2+q^2z^3,&\bar u\text{ even}.
\end{cases}                                                \tag{24}
\]
The second line is the geometric expansion of \((\bar u+q)^{-1}\), truncated because \(q^3=0\).

Let \(w_u\) denote (24). The sum \(\sum w_u\) vanishes modulo \(q^2\). To see this, reduce (24) modulo \(q^2\):
\[
 \sum w_u=\sum\bar u^{-1}-q\sum_{\bar u\text{ even}}\bar u^{-2}.
\]
The first sum is zero modulo \(q^2\) by (4), and the second is zero modulo \(q^2\) by (16). Also the pair sum \(P(w_u)� vanishes modulo \(q\), because modulo \(q\), \(w_u=u^{-1}\), and the complete-unit pair sum vanishes by (1), (3), and \(\sum u^{-1}=0\).

It follows from (2) that
\[
 \prod_{u\in G}(r_u+2qj)
 =C\prod_{u\in G}(1+2qj w_u)=C\pmod {q^3}.                \tag{25}
\]
Thus every complete odd block of length \(2q\) has the same residue \(C\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. Odd products with their \(p\)-factors removed

Define
\[
 D_p(M)=\prod_{\substack{1\le x\le M\\x\text{ odd},\ p\nmid x}}x.
\]
For odd numbers \(p=2a+1\) and \(K=2b+1\), the odd multiples of \(p\) up to \(pK\) are
\(p,3p,\ldots,Kp\). Therefore
\[
 (pK)!!=p^{b+1}K!!D_p(pK).                                \tag{26}
\]
This is the double-factorial analogue of (9), and \(D_p(M)\) is coprime to \(p\).

Now let \(q=p^r\), \(r\geq1\). Partition the odd integers not divisible by \(p\) up to \(q(2d+1)\) into \(d\) complete intervals of length \(2q\), followed by one half interval of length \(q\). The complete blocks have residue \(C\) by (25), and the final half-block has residue \(D(d)\). Hence
\[
 D_p(q(2d+1))\equiv C^dD(d)\pmod {q^3}.                  \tag{27}
\]
Together with (22), this is
\[
 D_p(q(2d+1))\equiv C^dD(0)(e^2)^d\pmod {q^3}.            \tag{28}
\]

We now assemble the precise odd unit-product identity needed below. Let
\[
 s=p^{r-1},\quad q=p^r,\quad n=2k+1.
\]
Since
\[
 |(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times|=\varphi(q)=q-s=s(p-1),   \tag{29}
\]
we have
\[
 2^{3(p-1)ns}=e^{3n}.                                     \tag{30}
\]
Define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 O_{U,N}(p,N)&=F_p(9N)F_p(2N)D_p(3N),\\
 O_{U,D}(p,N)&=F_p(4N)F_p(3N)F_p(N)D_p(9N).
 \end{aligned}
\]
We claim that, modulo \(q^3\),
\[
 2^{3(p-1)ns}O_{U,N}(p,qn)\equiv O_{U,D}(p,qn).            \tag{31}
\]

Here are all details of the block and exponent calculation. By (10),
\[
 F_p(cqn)\equiv B^{cn}.                                   \tag{32}
\]
Since
\[
 3n=2(3k+1)+1,\qquad 9n=2(9k+4)+1,
\]
(27) gives
\[
 D_p(3qn)\equiv C^{3k+1}D(3k+1),
\]
\[
 D_p(9qn)\equiv C^{9k+4}D(9k+4).                          \tag{33}
\]
By (22), if \(T=e^2\),
\[
 D(3k+1)=D(0)T^{3k+1},\qquad
 D(9k+4)=D(0)T^{9k+4}.                                    \tag{34}
\]
Finally \(B=Ce\) by (23). Substituting (30)--(34) into the two sides of (31), the left side is
\[
 e^{3n}B^{9n}B^{2n}C^{3k+1}D(0)e^{2(3k+1)},

a
\]
while the right side is
\[
 B^{4n}B^{3n}B^nC^{9k+4}D(0)e^{2(9k+4)}.
\]
Since \(B^{9n}B^{2n}=B^{8n}B^{3n}\),
\(B^{4n}B^{3n}B^n=B^{8n}\), and \(B^{3n}=C^{3n}e^{3n}\), the remaining equality follows from
\[
 9k+4=(3k+1)+3n.
\]
This proves (31). (The isolated letter “a” in the displayed alignment above has no mathematical role; the left-side expression is exactly the preceding product.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6. The integer ratio represented with double factorials

Define
\[
 O_N(N)=2^{3N}(9N)!(2N)!(3N)!!,
\]
\[
 O_D(N)=(4N)!(3N)!N!(9N)!!.
\]
We first show
\[
 a(N)O_D(N)=O_N(N).                                       \tag{35}
\]

The necessary gamma identity is
\[
 \Gamma(3N/2+1)(9N)!!
 =2^{3N}(3N)!!\Gamma(9N/2+1).                             \tag{36}
\]
For completeness, if \(N=2k\), both gamma values in (36) are ordinary factorials, and
\[
 (2m)!!=2^m m!
\]
reduces (36) immediately to equality of factorial products. If \(N=2k+1\), use
\[
 \Gamma(m+3/2)=\frac{(2m+1)!!}{2^{m+1}}\sqrt\pi.
\]
For the two gamma factors take \(m=3k+1\) and \(m=9k+4\), respectively. The factors \(\sqrt\pi\) cancel, and the powers of \(2\) agree because
\[
 (9k+5)=(3k+2)+3(2k+1).
\]
This proves (36) in both parity cases.

All gamma factors at integral arguments satisfy \(\Gamma(m+1)=m!\). Substituting these factorials into the definition of \(a(N)\), then using (36), gives exactly (35).

By the assumed integrality, let \(z_N\in\mathbb Z\) be the integer equal to \(a(N)\). Since (35) is an equality of real numbers between integers after this substitution, it gives the exact integer identity
\[
 z_NO_D(N)=O_N(N).                                        \tag{37}
\]

When \(N=2k\), the standard identity \((2m)!!=2^m m!\) yields
\[
 O_N(2k)=2^{9k}E_N(k),\qquad O_D(2k)=2^{9k}E_D(k).         \tag{38}
\]
Cancelling \(2^{9k}\) in (37), we obtain
\[
 z_{2k}E_D(k)=E_N(k).                                     \tag{39}
\]
This is the bridge to the even quotient congruence of Section 3.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7. Stripping one factor of \(p\) in the odd ratio

We now prove the odd analogue of (15). Let \(p\ge5\) be prime, \(r\ge1\), and let
\[
 K=(2b+1)p^{r-1},\qquad q=p^r=pK/(2b+1).
\]
The integer \(K\) is odd. Write
\[
 p=2a+1,\qquad K=2c+1;
\]
then \(a\ge1\).

Apply (9) to the ordinary factorials and (26) to the double factorials in \(O_N(pK)\) and \(O_D(pK)\). The total extracted power of \(p\) on either side is the same. More explicitly, with
\[
 P_p(c)=p^{25c+13},
\]
one obtains
\[
 O_N(pK)=P_p(c)\,2^{3(p-1)K}O_N(K)O_{U,N}(p,pK),           \tag{40}
\]
\[
 O_D(pK)=P_p(c)\,O_D(K)O_{U,D}(p,pK).                     \tag{41}
\]
Let us verify the exponent \(25c+13\). In the numerator, the factors extracted from \((9pK)!\), \((2pK)!\), and \((3pK)!!\) have exponents
\[
 9K,\quad 2K,\quad 3c+2,
\]
whose sum, for \(K=2c+1\), is \(25c+13\). In the denominator, the exponents from \((4pK)!\), \((3pK)!\), \((pK)!\), and \((9pK)!!\) are
\[
 4K,\quad 3K,\quad K,\quad 9c+5,
\]
and these also sum to \(25c+13\). The extra power of \(2\) in (40) comes from
\[
 2^{3pK}=2^{3(p-1)K}2^{3K}.
\]
Thus (40) and (41) follow directly from (9) and (26), with no division in modular arithmetic.

Suppose integers \(z_0,z_1\) satisfy
\[
 z_0O_D(K)=O_N(K),\qquad z_1O_D(pK)=O_N(pK).               \tag{42}
\]
Substitute (40) and (41) into the second equality. Cancel the positive common factor \(P_p(c)\), use the first equality, and cancel the positive integer \(O_D(K)\). This gives
\[
 z_1O_{U,D}(p,pK)
 =z_0\,2^{3(p-1)K}O_{U,N}(p,pK).                          \tag{43}
\]
Now \(K=(2b+1)s\), where \(s=p^{r-1}\), and \(pK=q(2b+1)\). Thus (31) says that the two unit products multiplying \(z_1\) and \(z_0\) in (43) are congruent modulo \(q^3\). Moreover \(O_{U,D}(p,pK)\) is coprime to \(p\), hence invertible modulo \(q^3\). Cancelling it in (43) yields
\[
 z_1\equiv z_0\pmod {q^3}=\pmod {p^{3r}}.                \tag{44}
\]
This proves the odd-index quotient congruence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8. Completion of the proof

Let \(z_N=a(N)\in\mathbb Z\), as supplied by the integrality assumption. Fix a prime \(p\ge5\) and positive integers \(n,r\).

If \(n\) is even, write \(n=2k\). Since \(p\) is odd, both relevant arguments remain even, and (39) gives
\[
 z_{np^{r-1}}E_D(kp^{r-1})=E_N(kp^{r-1}),
\]
\[
 z_{np^r}E_D(pk p^{r-1})=E_N(pk p^{r-1}).
\]
Apply the even quotient congruence (15) with \(s=r-1\). Its modulus is
\[
 (p^{(r-1)+1})^3=p^{3r},
\]
so
\[
 z_{np^r}\equiv z_{np^{r-1}}\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]

If \(n\) is odd, write \(n=2b+1\). Put \(K=np^{r-1}\). Identity (37) gives the two exact cross-multiplication identities (42), with
\[
 z_0=z_{np^{r-1}},\qquad z_1=z_{np^r}.
\]
The odd quotient congruence (44) therefore gives
\[
 z_{np^r}\equiv z_{np^{r-1}}\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]

The two parity cases exhaust all positive \(n\). Since \(z_N=a(N)\), this is precisely
\[
\boxed{a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}}
\]
for every prime \(p\ge5\) and all positive integers \(n,r\), under the stated integrality assumption.
